newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Vranitzky resigns after 10 years in power.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Vranitzky resigns after 10 years in power.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, Europe's second longest-serving government leader after Germany's Chancellor Helmut Kohl, resigned on Saturday and handed over power to his finance minister, Viktor Klima.
A relaxed but visibly tired Vranitzky made the surprise announcement after a two-hour emergency meeting of his Social Democratic Party, saying he was withdrawing completely from political life.

"I have informed the party leadership...of my decision to withdraw from my political posts as federal chancellor and head of the Social Democratic Party," Vranitzky, 59, told a crowd of reporters inside his party's headquarters in central Vienna.

"I thought that after so many years it would be a wise decision to transfer responsibility to younger people in the party. My friends in the (party leadership) have accepted, with some hesitation, but they accepted," he said.
President Thomas Klestil formally accepted Vranitzky's resignation and praised him for leading Austria through turbulent years since he became chancellor in June 1986.
"I have thanked him in the name of the Austrian republic...for his hard work and responsible leadership," Klestil told Austrian television.
Klestil said he hoped Klima would present his new cabinet lineup within the next few days. Constitutionally, the entire cabinet has to be sworn in anew alongside the new chancellor.
Klima, also a Social Democrat and long regarded as Vranitzky's heir apparent, has not yet been seen in public or made any statement.

The two men have worked closely together since Klima became finance minister in January last year, acting as a centre-left phalanx against their increasingly fractious coalition partner, the conservative People's Party led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel.
A clearly irritated Schuessel said he had only been informed of Vranitzky's plans just an hour before he announced his resignation.
"He did not inform us ahead of time as would have been customary," Schuessel said. "I was in Switzerland the whole day in my role as foreign minister, but would have been contactable at any time."

Schuessel, who is also vice chancellor, called for immediate coalition talks and said he wanted his party to remain in government. In an obvious sign of displeasure, Schuessel notably failed to make any comment on Vranitzky's years as government leader.
Their two parties have dominated Austria's post-World War Two politics but they have been at each other's throats over the past two years.

Outside Austria, Vranitzky may be best remembered for doing what no other Austrian chancellor had done before -- he paid an official visit to Israel in 1991 and said Austria, too, had been responsible for the horrors committed by Hitler's Nazi regime.
One of his most triumphant moments came in June 1994 when more than two thirds of the Austrian electorate voted in a referendum to join the European Union.

But his last two years in power have been marred by constant bickering with Schuessel's party and a slump in votes for the Social Democrats, largely in favour of the far-right Freedom Party led by populist Joerg Haider.
Vranitzky's party suffered its worst election result in a European election last October when political obituary writers began sharpening their pens.
The chancellor then dismissed speculation over his imminent resignation, saying he would remain as party leader until Austria's next scheduled general election in 1999.

But a coalition crisis last weekend over the sale of the country's second-biggest bank Creditanstalt to Bank Austria, which was opposed by Schuessel, may have been the final straw to break Vranitzky's back.
